# What the Architect Owns {#sec-what-architect-owns}

![](images/ch11-cover-map.svg){fig-alt="Substantial AI-native design work and architectural ownership remain distinct from a named commitment authority inside an accountable organization."}

::: {.epigraph}
> "The second irony is that the designer who tries to eliminate the operator still leaves the operator to do the tasks which the designer cannot think how to automate."
>
> — Lisanne Bainbridge, *Ironies of Automation* (1983) [@Bainbridge1983Ironies, p. 775]
:::

::: {.column-margin}
**Author's Note.** Lisanne Bainbridge, an industrial psychologist who studied automated plant operations, observed that automation does not eliminate human operators; it leaves them the critical edge cases while the skills those cases demand decay from disuse. As generative models handle register-transfer level (RTL) generation and simulation sweeps, our role as architects shifts from routine execution to cross-layer failure diagnosis, screening non-recurring engineering (NRE) capital risk, and forming supported tapeout recommendations for a named commitment authority.
:::

Grant the strongest case for automation. An AI-native design system can formulate studies, generate syntactically clean register-transfer level (RTL) netlists, navigate high-dimensional microarchitectural spaces, run closed-loop toolchains (@sec-running-the-loop), and recommend candidate tapeouts. If automation can shoulder these routine and specialized tasks, what core technical work do human architects still contribute?

Architectural ownership does not reside in a shrinking enclave of residual tasks that automation has not yet absorbed. When generative models draft synthesizable Verilog and automated electronic design automation (EDA) loops run closed-loop optimization, engineering organizations face a temptation to treat the human architect as an expensive bottleneck to design out of the loop. Industrial systems engineering shows why this strategy backfires. Automating routine execution leaves human engineers solely responsible for anomalous, cross-layer failures that defy formalization, while stripping them of the daily diagnostic contact needed to resolve those edge cases [@Bainbridge1983Ironies]. In semiconductor design, the equivalent failure is an opaque optimization loop burying a cross-layer physical defect that escapes pre-silicon screening and surfaces only after committing $\$120\ \text{million}$ to reticle masks. The essential difficulty of engineering lies in specifying system intent and physical boundaries rather than in generating intermediate representations [@Brooks1986NoSilverBullet]. Organizational ownership must therefore preserve the architect's diagnostic engagement even as execution accelerates.

Human technical contribution centers on five nondelegable cross-layer governance responsibilities:

1. *Framing system boundaries* across the eight requirement domains (@sec-intent-vs-spec).
2. *Adjudicating cross-stack trade-offs* between competing domain specialists and conflicting tool returns.
3. *Managing irreversible capital risk*, recognizing that while automation compresses front-end engineering labor, fixed reticle mask charges ($\$120\ \text{million}$ at 3\ nm) fall due unchanged at tapeout.
4. *Designing and verifying hardware containment mechanisms* (such as programmable microcode chicken-bits) that preserve declared requirements under tested derated conditions.
5. *Forming a supported technical recommendation* for a named commitment authority within an accountable organization.

Delegating execution to automated design loops accelerates search, but the architect must retain technical contact, separating empirical specialist evidence from organizational tapeout commitments.

<!-- AUTHOR-THESIS DRAFT 2026-08-31: contract clause "grant the strongest plausible AI"; the chapter argued largely from AI weakness and never said which arguments survive a system that can also diagnose the failure -->
The case for that separation should not rest on what today's systems cannot do. Suppose the design system can read the waveform, localize a power-delivery droop to the burst pattern that causes it, and propose the containment itself. The diagnostic argument for the architect then weakens, and it was never the load-bearing one. Two arguments survive a system of any capability. A commitment is an act by a party who can be held to account for the consequence, not an inference drawn from evidence, and no quantity of evidence converts itself into that act. The problem is chosen by whoever bears the product consequence of solving the wrong one, and a system that solves whatever it is handed cannot choose what it is handed. Diagnostic contact matters because it keeps those two acts informed; the accountable choice of problem and the accountable commitment are what the rest of this chapter governs.
<!-- END DRAFT -->

::: {.callout-learning-objectives}
This chapter establishes the following learning objectives:

- **Frame** coherent architecture problems across the eight requirement domains and select the abstractions and system boundaries that govern a freeze decision.
- **Synthesize** cross-disciplinary specialist evidence across central processing unit (CPU) cores, neural processing unit (NPU) accelerators, memory hierarchies, and 2.5D packaging into a unified system recommendation.
- **Resolve** cross-layer discrepancies using structured protocols (contract alignment, abstraction correction, escalation) while decoupling empirical program claims from executive capital commitments.
- **Structure** the handoff from execution and scoped support through the architect's system recommendation to a named commitment authority, enforcing clean-room IP provenance and immutable verification trails.
- **Manage** irreversible capital risk by stating residual risk, evaluating scoped containment, and keeping commitment open when required evidence is missing.
:::

## Delegating Without Losing Technical Contact {#sec-delegating-without-losing-contact}

In Architecture 1.0, engineers manually constructed microarchitectural blocks, wrote RTL, and iteratively executed point EDA tools, developing tacit familiarity with waveform behaviors, routing congestion, and timing slack margins. Architecture 2.0 shifts this workflow by delegating candidate drafting, macro floorplanning, and regression sweeps to automated methods. When practitioners interact with silicon design solely through high-level scorecards, their physical debugging intuition atrophies, leaving them unable to diagnose anomalous failures when automated tools derail. If governance degrades to rubber-stamping generated proposals, the human architect becomes legally and organizationally liable for uninspected machine errors. Preserving architectural ownership requires structuring human-in-the-loop interfaces that maintain deep diagnostic contact and enforce a named, nondelegable commitment authority without bottlenecking machine-speed search.

::: {.callout-law title="Moral Crumple Zones and Nondelegable Signoff"}
The human operator in an automated system becomes the *moral crumple zone* when they absorb liability for failures generated by automation they could not meaningfully inspect or halt [@Elish2019MoralCrumpleZones; @Bainbridge1983Ironies]. The antidote is a named human commitment authority backed by inspectable evidence packages and explicit residual risk declarations (@sec-law-moral-crumple-zones in @sec-appendix-c-laws-paradoxes).
:::

To prevent architects from becoming moral crumple zones, engineering organizations must partition technical delegation from signoff authority across the design stack. At Layer 3 (@fig-ch01-three-layers-ai-integration), where the system coordinates multi-tool exploration and verification across the vertical stack, the human architect still defines the system problem, selects abstractions, resolves cross-layer discrepancies, and declares residual risk before a named commitment authority decides whether the organization commits to an irreversible tapeout transition.

Because organizational assignments vary across projects, four engineering responsibilities remain structurally separate. The integration of these roles forms the foundation of the in-order commitment model (@fig-architecture-synthesis-commitment). First, automated tools and domain specialists generate and qualify results within focused disciplines, owning localized verification signoffs. Second, architects integrate these isolated results into a unified system design, framing cross-layer trade-offs and declaring residual risk. Third, a named commitment authority evaluates the architect's supported recommendation to decide whether the organization advances the design to a subsequent project phase. Finally, the accountable organization provisions resources for these functions and owns the real-world product consequences. *In order* means that specification changes, constraint waivers, and promotions to the common baseline receive an architect's current recommendation and a recorded authority decision in strict serial order, even when exploration proceeds in parallel. One person may occupy both the architect and commitment-authority functions only when the record identifies which function is being exercised, preserves their distinct rights and responsibilities, and keeps independent checks and organizational accountability explicit. This separation prevents a successful local tool run from silently authorizing a global tapeout.

![**Cross-layer technical synthesis precedes organizational tapeout commitment.** Domain specialists qualify scoped results and checks across CPU, NPU, memory, and packaging layers. Architects frame problems, choose abstractions and system boundaries, connect physical and logical layers, interpret disagreements, and declare residual risk before presenting a supported technical recommendation. A functionally separate commitment authority advances, holds, or rejects the design within an accountable organization.](images/fig-architecture-synthesis-commitment){#fig-architecture-synthesis-commitment width="100%" fig-alt="An accountable organization surrounds three distinct roles. Domain specialists qualify scoped results, checks, artifacts, and failures. Architects frame the problem, choose abstractions and system boundaries, connect layers, interpret disagreements, state residual risk, and retain access to decisive artifacts and failures. The supported technical recommendation reaches a functionally separate commitment authority that advances, holds, or rejects the design. Continuous monitoring and changed conditions return to architects and may reopen specialist work."}

This operational separation ensures that raw specialist data is synthesized before executive commitment, preventing commitment authorities from approving tapeout decisions by mere implication. When the architect interprets conflicting specialist results and scopes residual risk, they provide the commitment authority with a bounded, actionable recommendation rather than an overwhelming dump of simulation logs. NASA's systems engineering guidance provides a precedent for this structural separation, emphasizing the production of analytical comparisons and formal recommendations for a distinct decision-making authority [@NASA2017SystemsEngineeringHandbook, sec. 6.8]. This structural clarity preserves the architect's technical judgment while reserving irreversible capital deployment for the named commitment authority.

Delegating tasks without forfeiting ownership requires satisfying four boundary conditions:

1. **Observability:** candidate state remains directly inspectable.
2. **Reversibility:** proposed changes can be rolled back cleanly.
3. **Independent checks:** bad results are caught by independent verification rather than self-evaluation.
4. **Bounded consequences:** cross-layer interactions are explicitly delimited.

A bounded array mapping sweep or focused tool run satisfies these criteria, enabling execution delegation while retaining oversight. Conversely, freezing an instruction set architecture (ISA) contract or fixing the PHY lane count on a 2.5D Universal Chiplet Interconnect Express (UCIe) link hardens assumptions across compiler runtimes, memory hierarchies, RTL, floorplans, and product thermals. In such high-irreversibility transitions, evidence gathered across coupled layers must be reconciled before the commitment authority authorizes the freeze.

Preserving engineering coherence requires maintaining direct technical contact across tool boundaries. Human factors research distinguishes *misuse* (inappropriate reliance on automation) from *disuse* (neglecting automation capabilities entirely) [@ParasuramanRiley1997HumansAutomation]. Historical shifts in design abstraction [@DeMicheli1994SynthesisOptimization; @Izraelevitz2017Chisel] succeeded because engineers retained deep diagnostic capabilities: the ability to challenge formulations, inspect decisive failure traces, and recognize when models operate outside their valid support. As automated loops absorb routine microarchitectural sweeps, the architect's work centers on defining problem boundaries, enforcing cross-layer interface invariants, and evaluating whether combined empirical evidence justifies hardware commitment.

The same delegation opens an apprenticeship gap. Junior engineers who meet silicon only through prompts and scorecards never acquire the diagnostic exposure a future commitment authority needs, and how a discipline trains that judgment is a shared problem taken up in @sec-curriculum-certification.

::: {.callout-design-principle title="Judgment Precedes and Governs Automation"}
**The principle:** While automation may handle local formulation, exploration, implementation, and analysis, architectural judgment dictates the problem, the abstraction, and the system boundaries.

**The application:** Every design review must identify the architect responsible for the supported recommendation, the commitment authority responsible for the organizational decision, and how isolated results unite to form one feasible system.
:::

## Framing Cross-Layer Problems {#sec-framing-architecture-problem}

Exercising architectural ownership begins long before an automated optimizer executes a single pass. Before search algorithms evaluate candidates or optimizers tune subblocks, architects must define the system boundary, identify governing cross-layer interactions, and determine which physical consequences studies must expose. Defining mechanisms, interfaces, and fallback strategies frames the design space itself [@PattersonDitzel1980RISC]. Beyond bounding the physical system, architects design the complete decision workflow: selecting methods to propose candidate modifications, modeling tools to measure properties, validation checks to screen candidates, and protocols to resolve cross-layer disagreements.

The Lighthouse prompt, "Design a low-power, 64-bit RISC-V-based compute subsystem for a real-time mobile extended-reality (XR) workload," was decomposed across the eight requirement domains in @sec-intent-vs-spec. A freeze decision adds to that decomposition what exploration never needed. Studying array utilization requires cycle-level modeling and mapping search; freezing that array alongside its software interface and UCIe packaging link demands far more. The architect must provision instruments capturing compiler lowering across Triton, LLVM, and Multi-Level Intermediate Representation (MLIR) passes, memory traffic, UCIe physical layer latency, physical timing at the signoff corners, total 3\ W subsystem thermal design power (TDP), IP indemnification, NRE capital review, and modification consequences. The specific architecture question drives the selection of these abstractions and bounds the required evidence.

Bounding that evidence takes eight recurring judgments that turn isolated results into one recommendation (@tbl-architect-technical-judgments). They force the architect to declare missing constraints, adjudicate cross-layer trade-offs, and state residual risk, so that the commitment decision rests on a physically grounded picture of the system rather than on localized optimism.

| **Judgment** | **Architectural question** | **Lighthouse consequence** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Problem choice and reframing** | Is the stated problem still the one the product needs solved? | Deciding whether the goal is maximizing raw NPU general matrix multiply (GEMM) utilization or satisfying the strict 120\ frames per second (FPS) mobile XR latency budget within a 3\ W TDP envelope. |
| **Abstraction** | Which details can be simplified for this decision? | A cycle-level NPU model can compare matrix mappings locally, but it cannot hide Triton/LLVM/MLIR compiler lowering, static random-access memory (SRAM) / LPDDR5 memory traffic, UCIe interconnect energy, physical timing, or the 3\ W subsystem boundary from a freeze decision. |
| **System boundary** | Where do workload, software, hardware, package, physical design, and product effects meet? | Deciding whether NPU array sizing can be analyzed in isolation, or must encompass host RV64GCV task dispatch, UCIe chiplet routing, dynamic random-access memory (DRAM) bandwidth contention, and packaging thermal limits. |
| **Architecture synthesis** | Do chosen mechanisms, interfaces, software paths, and implementation choices form one feasible system? | Confirming that the NPU matrix engine, RV64GCV CPU contract, compiler lowering pipeline, LPDDR5 memory subsystem, and firmware fallback paths form a coherent, manufacturable subsystem. |
| **Missing constraints** | What has the formulation, representation, or tool path left out? | Uncovering omitted physical and legal factors: transient power delivery network (PDN) voltage droop ($di/dt$), 3\ W thermal dissipation limits, UCIe signal integrity, IP indemnification, and hardware chicken-bit fallbacks. |
| **Cross-layer trade-off** | Which feasible point best serves the product when objectives conflict? | Resolving the tension between host RV64GCV vector tail latency, NPU matrix throughput, LPDDR5 memory power, UCIe die-to-die routing congestion, and manual review burden. |
| **Mechanism and consequence** | Does the proposed explanation fit the observations, and what happens if it is wrong? | Evaluating whether an apparent speedup is driven by architectural dataflow or an unmodeled memory wait state, where an erroneous tapeout freeze risks multimillion-dollar silicon mask respins. |
| **Commitment under uncertainty** | Are remaining risks understood, containable, and worth accepting? | Recommending against physical tapeout when static timing closure, formal property bounds, IP indemnification, and power delivery margins remain uncharacterized. |
: **Architecture judgment gives technical work its system meaning.** Architects choose the question, abstraction, boundary, and consequence before the commitment authority decides whether the design advances. {#tbl-architect-technical-judgments tbl-colwidths="[22,38,40]"}

These judgments collectively ensure that feasibility claims do not collapse when abstractions omit physical coupling. For example, reconciling a 120\ FPS XR rendering target with a 3\ W thermal envelope requires tracing how NPU direct memory access (DMA) burst sizing affects LPDDR5 bus contention, host CPU interrupt latency, and package thermal gradients before committing to tapeout. When physical interactions cross subsystem boundaries, simplified abstractions hide bottlenecks that manifest only during full-system physical signoff.

## Selecting System Abstractions and Bounds {#sec-selecting-abstractions-constraints}

Once system boundaries are declared, the architect must choose the representations and analytical models that govern exploration. Every architectural model is defined as much by what it omits as by what it represents. Selecting an architectural abstraction decides which physical details govern the current decision and which can be safely set aside. The same chip candidate can be modeled as an abstract syntax tree (AST), a control-data flow graph (CDFG), or an MLIR pass. It can appear as a host CPU instruction stream in gem5, an NPU tensor dataflow in SCALE-Sim, or a memory trace in Ramulator. Further down the stack, it becomes synthesizable RTL in Verilator, gate-level netlists in Yosys governed by Unified Power Format (UPF) rules, a 2.5D UCIe chiplet layout in OpenROAD, or a thermal dissipation map. None of these views constitutes the complete architecture on its own. Because every representation illuminates specific cross-layer relationships while obscuring others, architects must select models whose omissions do not silently invalidate the design action under review.

::: {.column-margin}
**Architecture description standards.** ISO/IEC/Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers (IEEE) 42010 distinguishes an entity architecture from an architecture description that expresses it. The standard specifies requirements for architecture viewpoints and model kinds, but it does not prescribe this book's chapter structure, a team's specific design process, or the organizational assignment of commitment authority [@ISOIECIEEE2022ArchitectureDescription].
:::

Abstraction choice dictates which components contribute to a design decision. Architects must determine what architectural state each predictor, generator, optimizer, or tool is allowed to modify and which observations constrain those changes. Aggregating optimized blocks does not yield a viable system if internal abstractions hide blocking physical effects such as power delivery network (PDN) voltage droop or die-to-die thermal coupling. AlphaChip illustrates this contrast in semiconductor macro placement [@MirhoseiniEtAl2021GraphPlacement]. An automated macro-placement tool can optimize an NPU floorplan locally, but its objective function omits PDN $IR$-drop transients that starve neighboring CPU cores or exceed local thermal dissipator limits across a 2.5D UCIe link. Architects define block boundaries, curate macro sets, establish timing and power constraints across host CPU and NPU cores, determine comparison baselines, and execute physical signoff checks.

Architects also structure component interaction by defining interface contracts, assigning revision authority, selecting independent signoff checks, and auditing shared assumptions across verification steps. Consequential constraints often originate as tacit engineering knowledge [@Polanyi1966TacitDimension, p. 4]. Compiler leads may know a matrix opcode lacks an efficient lowering path, while physical design leads may recognize power-grid heuristics that fail on dense CPU-NPU layouts. Language models can assist in locating, comparing, and organizing scattered expert judgments for formal review, but consequential constraints and assumptions require checks commensurate with their risk and scope, delegated to automated checkers, conventional EDA tools, domain specialists, or peer reviewers. If accepted, constraints must record their source, scope, affected interfaces, known conflicts, and reopening triggers.

A physical designer's rule against placing two high-current macros on the same power stripe provides qualifying geometry and operating thresholds; architects decide how to enforce it and evaluate routing overhead. Shifting to a new power-grid template or 3D stacked die invalidates the basis of the rule, triggering formal review rather than leaving obsolete constraints in force. Unrecorded constraints risk being optimized away, while overgeneralized constraints reject valid designs; navigating this trade-off allows composing individual components, evaluation tools, and specialist judgments into a cohesive architectural system.

## Governing System Integration {#sec-orchestrating-system-integration}

A design candidate transitions from an assortment of isolated optimizations into a viable architecture only when its mechanisms and interfaces hold together under the physical and logical realities of the full system stack. Automated tools and domain specialists deliver local optimizations within bounded disciplines, but point optimizers cannot evaluate how aggressive NPU array layouts affect host CPU cache coherence, memory channel contention, or UCIe chiplet thermal dissipation. The architect's task is composing specialized results into a unified system decision, exposing unexamined cross-layer interactions across domain boundaries.

Consider a hypothetical revision of the Lighthouse XR system-on-chip (SoC). Trace analyses in gem5 and SCALE-Sim support the target frame rate, MLIR compiler searches yield legal NPU tiling, Verilator RTL simulations pass, Ramulator memory models satisfy local bandwidth checks, OpenSTA closes timing, and UPF checks validate power-gating boundaries. Although each check passes in isolation, combining results exposes cross-layer faults. NPU tiling increases burst memory traffic, pushing SRAM arrays, UCIe links, and LPDDR5 channels beyond the 3\ W thermal envelope, while a critical tail-latency path lacks software fallback.

Synthesizing a working solution requires coordinated cross-layer adjustments. The architect assigns tail-latency handling to the host CPU core, narrows NPU DMA bursts, rebalances memory buffers, and specifies firmware fallback paths. If post-silicon validation reveals DMA race conditions, microcode *chicken-bits* (programmable control register overrides that disable problematic speculative paths) quarantine the bug without forcing an immediate respin. Iterating on mechanisms, interfaces, and partitioning unites specialized results into a feasible product.

Architects thread these outputs together, from high-level XR workloads down through tensor tiling, interconnect traffic, memory buffering, thermal envelopes, and software fallback mechanisms. This synthesis produces an actionable recommendation bounded by an explicit scope, detailing supporting and conflicting results alongside known limits. Domain-level checks qualify what recommendations support; they do not authorize product commitment.

## Resolving Cross-Layer Discrepancies {#sec-resolving-discrepancies}

Composing multi-domain models frequently surfaces direct contradictions across tool boundaries. A cycle-level simulator may report performance gains for a new NPU array mapping while physical signoff tools report power-grid voltage drops under host CPU vector loads. Architectural judgment is tested when qualified specialist checks contradict one another. When domain results conflict, metrics cannot be averaged or selected based on schedule pressure. Advancing the design requires explaining the underlying physical mechanism driving the conflict, reexamining abstractions, requesting discriminating experiments, or keeping transitions blocked until discrepancies resolve.

When specialist tools contradict one another, engineering teams resolve discrepancies through a disciplined three-stage protocol:

1. **Contract and condition alignment:** Domain specialists determine whether conflicting checks encode identical contracts and operating conditions. If they do, a blocking failure remains an unconditional failure.
2. **Abstraction correction:** If checks evaluate mismatched contracts, the architectural abstraction or interface definition must be corrected and affected tool paths rerun.
3. **Escalation under unresolved scope:** When specialists cannot reconcile scopes within allocated budgets, the transition remains blocked and the unresolved system contract is escalated to the commitment authority.

Consider a coherence verifier using SystemVerilog Assertions (SVA) evaluated via bounded model checking (BMC) returning a counterexample against a declared blocking property between host CPU caches and NPU DMA stores up to bound $k = 50$ cycles, while a high-level software model treats execution as legal under high-contention LPDDR5 traffic. The property cannot be weakened, the failing workload discarded, or the counterexample recast as passing. The technical question is whether formal properties and software models encode identical product contracts. If they do, the candidate fails; if not, the architecture contract must be corrected and both paths rerun.

When feasible candidates exhibit overlapping estimates for tail latency and subsystem power, architects identify whether workload sampling, model error, or untested operating corners could reverse the choice. The appropriate response is requesting the least costly higher-fidelity observation capable of discriminating between them (matched cycle-level trace runs in gem5, physical thermal simulations, OpenSTA static timing runs, or implementation-facing power-grid analyses). If available observations cannot resolve overlap within budget, recommendations remain narrow and choices reversible.

## Separating Evidence from Commitments {#sec-linking-results-claims-commitments}

Resolving technical discrepancies yields qualified evidence, but evidence alone never authorizes capital expenditure. A validated simulation report or benchmark comparison does not constitute a decision to tape out silicon. Technical synthesis yields a supported architectural recommendation, distinct from organizational commitment to manufacture hardware. Recommendations present preferred candidates alongside evaluated alternatives, document boundary conditions and signoff checks, and explicitly expose residual uncertainties. Domain specialists retain sole ownership over their domain signoffs in timing closure, power integrity, physical implementation, and reliability.

The two independent tests from @sec-moonshot structure the separation between technical evidence and project commitment:

1. **Evidence test (program claim):** Did the complete approach improve the architecture result or reduce total cost to reach a comparable result? (Classified as *supported*, *unsupported*, or *unresolved*.)
2. **Decision test (architecture commitment):** Does the named commitment authority, weighing trade-offs, result limits, and residual risk, decide that the work justifies commitment?

Generating qualified results, formulating system recommendations, and executing authorized decisions are distinct architectural actions that cannot substitute for one another. A favorable simulation output does not mandate a tapeout. To maintain organizational accountability, the program claim status and the hardware commitment must decouple completely (@tbl-two-closing-decisions).

| **Program claim status** | **What it means for architecture commitment** |
| --- | --- |
| **Supported** | Repeated matched comparisons across declared tasks and conditions clear the decision boundary. The organization may still reject the hardware architecture if physical thermals, supporting evidence, organizational capacity, or residual risks remain unacceptable. |
| **Unsupported** | Matched comparisons demonstrate the claimed workflow advantage fails to clear core decision criteria. The organization may still commit to a structurally sound architecture if supported by conventional engineering evidence. |
| **Unresolved** | Comparisons are missing, incomplete, or underpowered, blocking adoption claims. The organization proceeds with hardware commitment only when backed by independent, high-fidelity design checks. |
: **Program claim status and architecture commitment remain independent.** A favorable result on one cannot substitute for a favorable result on the other in architectural methodologies. {#tbl-two-closing-decisions tbl-colwidths="[28,72]"}

## Governing Tapeout Commitments {#sec-governing-tapeout-commitments}

When evidence is systematically separated from commitments, the organization must structure how that final commitment is exercised. As designs advance from high-level exploration to physical silicon, commitments steadily narrow reversibility. Committing freezes interfaces, bus contracts, and floorplans. Early in design cycles, modifying ISA extensions or buffer layouts requires editing software models or RTL. In contrast, modifying package substrate routing and reticle masks after freeze costs millions of dollars and months of delay. As reversibility decreases, the required standard of empirical evidence rises proportionally.

::: {.callout-war-story title="Declining to commit is a decision, and it is made by someone"}
**The claim.** Intel's Larrabee described a many-core x86 architecture for visual computing, with wide vector units, coherent caches, and a software renderer in place of most fixed-function graphics hardware [@SeilerEtAl2008Larrabee]. The design was published, the silicon existed, and the architectural argument was serious.

**The gap.** The performance the product needed against shipping discrete graphics parts did not arrive on the schedule the market required. Intel withdrew the consumer graphics product while continuing the line as a throughput-computing part, which is a different commitment supported by different evidence.

**The lesson.** No result forced that outcome and no metric selected it. People with the authority to spend the next increment of capital read what the evidence supported, decided it did not support the product they had planned, and said so. An architecture program that cannot produce that decision, and cannot name who owns it, has no way to stop.
:::

Commitment records define which design advances, which alternatives were rejected, which conditions evidence covered, what uncertainty remains, and what triggers would invalidate the choice. To systematically capture this information, engineering authority must be explicitly divided into three distinct decision tiers (@tbl-lighthouse-action-rights). This framework separates the tactical execution of design work, the analytical support provided by verification results, and the strategic commitment of capital.

| **Decision** | **Technical question** | **Boundary** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Execute design work** | What candidate state may this person, model, or tool change, and when must it stop? | Work stays within the declared design space, interfaces, budget, and evaluator boundary. |
| **Establish what a result supports** | What does this check show about this artifact under these conditions and assumptions? | Domain specialists own result validity and domain scope. The architect determines how that result applies to the system decision. |
| **Commit the architecture** | Does the integrated design justify the next consequential transition (e.g., tapeout freeze)? | The named commitment authority decides after considering the architect's system recommendation, alternatives, cross-layer results, specialist concurrences, uncertainty, and residual risk. |
: **Execution, support, and commitment remain distinctly separate action rights.** Separating these decision tiers prevents a successful tool run or a favorable local result from silently authorizing a system architecture. {#tbl-lighthouse-action-rights tbl-colwidths="[28,34,38]"}

Classic human-automation frameworks separate information acquisition, analysis, decision selection, and action implementation [@ParasuramanEtAl2000LevelsAutomation], which directly reinforces the necessity of decoupling execution, support, and commitment. Enforcing these boundaries prevents automated components from overstepping their execution mandate and accidentally triggering physical commitments. Completed check records remain immutable; subsequent judgments cannot rewrite past results.

If operating conditions shift or new physical constraints emerge, earlier results may become inapplicable, requiring fresh evidence rather than altering historical logs. This immutability guarantees that every architecture commitment is backed by a verifiable, point-in-time chain of evidence, providing a clear audit trail when diagnosing post-silicon anomalies.

### IP Provenance and Indemnification

Before committing capital to silicon fabrication, the commitment authority must satisfy legal and IP indemnification standards. Generative models trained on public open-source code repositories risk regurgitating copyleft-licensed (e.g., GPL-3.0) RTL modules or patented microarchitectural circuits into commercial SoC designs.

To establish defensible IP provenance, the AI-native design system maintains a clean-room verification trail:

- **Cryptographic Prompt and Lineage Logs:** Every prompt, tool execution transcript, and intermediate AST representation is timestamped and cryptographically signed (`sha256`), proving that candidate RTL originated from declared system intent rather than unrecorded copy-paste ingestion. Clean-room provenance logs document internal design derivation and absence of verbatim copying, but do not automatically guarantee patent non-infringement; commercial tapeouts combine internal lineage logs with enterprise IP indemnification contracts to manage residual third-party infringement exposure.
- **Code Similarity and License Scanners:** Synthesized RTL blocks pass through automated code similarity engines (such as Black Duck or FossID) to screen for verbatim overlap with public copyrighted repositories before entering the tapeout codebase.
- **Foundry NDA Air-Gap Compliance:** Verification audits confirm that proprietary foundry process design kit (PDK) rules, cell libraries, and internal interconnect protocols were processed strictly within secure on-premises compute enclaves and never transmitted to external cloud large language model (LLM) providers.
- **Third-Party Commercial IP Enclaves:** Automated methods must treat vendor-licensed hard and soft IP blocks (such as memory PHYs, PCIe controllers, high-speed SerDes, and analog phase-locked loops) as immutable black boxes with pinned interface contracts. System exploration is restricted to top-level interconnects and custom accelerator logic, preventing unauthorized modification or leakage of vendor intellectual property under strict licensing agreements.

### Managing Residual Risk with Hardware Chicken-Bits

Committing under uncertainty requires understanding failure modes well enough to accept, mitigate, or block them. Residual risk is an inherent technical property of a decision, not an administrative label. Usable residual risk statements specify five core elements:

1. **Failure mode:** explicit physical mechanism (such as dynamic $IR$-drop power collapse during bursty tensor execution, asynchronous clock-domain crossing (CDC) metastability races, or uncharacterized setup timing waivers).
2. **Consequence:** impact on performance, power, thermals, data integrity, or safety.
3. **Remaining uncertainty:** quantified bounds on unknown factors.
4. **Detecting check:** empirical test, telemetry signal, or monitor assigned to observe the mode.
5. **Containment action:** verified fallback path, throttling mechanism, or hardware chicken-bit.

In hardware design, containment operates across two distinct timescales. Permanent hardware e-fuses (blown during wafer sort or packaging) disable unverified IP blocks or isolate defective array columns. Firmware-managed chicken-bits (software-writable control and status registers protected by privileged architectural modes) allow boot firmware to bypass speculative microarchitectural optimizations or insert cycle wait states upon detecting transient voltage droop post-silicon. The following author-constructed Lighthouse teaching example illustrates how a commitment review might represent such controls. The names, behaviors, and values are illustrative rather than measured or deployed results:

- **Chicken-Bit 0 (`DIS_SPEC_STORE_FWD`):** Disables speculative load bypassing around uncommitted store buffer entries, forcing dependent memory operations to wait until prior stores commit, eliminating transient ordering races.
- **Chicken-Bit 1 (`FORCE_L1_WRITETHROUGH`):** Forces conservative L1 data cache write-through mode, bypassing dirty writeback buffering to prevent cache-line corruption under unstable low-voltage retention.
- **Chicken-Bit 2 (`INJECT_NPU_WAITSTATES`):** Injects programmable 2-cycle wait states on the matrix accumulator result bus during high-toggle execution, dampening peak $di/dt$ current transients and preventing resonant ground bounce.

A commitment record for a speculative microarchitectural optimization should state the performance cost of its proposed fallback. This teaching example represents that cost as a pre-silicon *derating penalty*:

$$
\Delta_{\text{derate}} = \frac{T_{\text{derated}} - T_{\text{nominal}}}{T_{\text{nominal}}}
$$

In this constructed example, asserting `INJECT_NPU_WAITSTATES` is assumed to incur $\Delta_{\text{derate}} = +12\%$ latency on dense matrix operations. That assumed penalty defines one declared derated envelope for the example; it is not an empirical processor result. Before relying on the fallback, the commitment review must verify its behavior under the relevant failure mode and determine whether the 120\ FPS XR frame deadline and 3\ W TDP budget still hold under the declared envelope. The review must also establish which controls can legally operate together rather than assuming that every chicken-bit can be asserted simultaneously.

Under the example's assumptions, activating the wait-state control could cause the candidate to miss its product target. Passing the scoped derated check would establish only that the declared fallback remains within the requirements and conditions actually tested. It would not guarantee commercial viability or isolate all financial risk. The architect records that technical limit in the recommendation, and the named commitment authority decides whether the remaining risk justifies tapeout.

<!-- AUTHOR-THESIS DRAFT 2026-08-31: the five-element residual-risk statement was never filled in end to end; this instantiates it from the chapter's own constructed Lighthouse material, no new numbers -->
Written out for the constructed Lighthouse case, the five elements read as one record rather than a list. The failure mode is peak $di/dt$ current transients on the matrix accumulator result bus during dense GEMM execution, driving PDN voltage droop below the retention margin of the L1 data arrays. The consequence is silent cache-line corruption on the host path and, if the droop trips a throttle, a missed 120\ FPS frame deadline inside the 3\ W envelope. The remaining uncertainty is that no dynamic $IR$-drop analysis under the declared activity and package assumptions has been run, so the droop magnitude and its onset activity level are unbounded before silicon, and the assumed $\Delta_{\text{derate}} = +12\%$ is an assumption rather than a characterization. The detecting checks are dynamic $IR$-drop analysis before freeze and, after silicon, error-correcting code (ECC) error counts on the affected arrays together with the NPU throttle and reset signatures that operating teams already track. The containment action is `INJECT_NPU_WAITSTATES`, accepted only once its disabled and asserted states are verified under the active droop, its legal combination with `FORCE_L1_WRITETHROUGH` is established, and the derated envelope is shown to hold the frame deadline. A record that cannot fill one of the five lines is not ready for the commitment authority.
<!-- END DRAFT -->

Consider an uncharacterized vector turbo mode on an NPU. Retaining unverified circuitry does not justify production enablement. Crafting a defensible exception requires a verified disabled state, an enable path restricted to authorized lab modes, verified reset and fault handling, proof that disabled circuitry does not violate baseline requirements, a named owner, and a firm expiration tied to post-silicon characterization. Unchecked exceptions risk normalizing deviance [@Vaughan1996Challenger], and the risk compounds once the components that generate candidates can also edit the files an exception lives in.

The governance that closes that path is mechanical rather than cultural. The generator and optimizer hold read-only access to the timing constraint files, the UPF power-intent specification, and the waiver registry, so no search loop can relax a constraint to make its own candidate close. Every waiver, timing exception, and false-path declaration carries an out-of-band cryptographic signature from a named signoff authority, sits in an immutable version-controlled record, and states the criterion that retires it, whether a post-silicon characterization, a signoff-corner run, or a date. That signature is the recorded authority decision the in-order commit model requires for a constraint change. A waiver that cannot name its own expiration is a permanent baseline change in disguise, and the commitment review treats it as one.

Containment mechanisms (hardware feature-disable fuses, firmware fallbacks, thermal derating modes, redundant UCIe lanes, memory isolation boundaries) must be verified extensively. If no credible containment lever exists, the tapeout commitment must be refused outright. Disable mechanisms are not universal insurance policies; the commitment review must verify the disabled state, isolate the failure from required behavior, and confirm that the control path remains available even under the active fault being contained.

Advancing a candidate architecture from software simulation to physical silicon commits irreversible non-recurring engineering (NRE) capital. This irreversible financial step makes the evaluation of whether power, performance, and area (PPA) gains justify fixed mask charges a core commitment responsibility (@fig-nre-mask-cost-productivity). While an AI-native design system can compress front-end engineering labor costs through rapid generation and evaluation, reticle mask charges remain fixed physical capital expenditures that fall due upon mask freeze regardless of synthesis speed.

```{python}
#| label: fig-nre-mask-cost-productivity
#| fig-cap: |
#|   **Front-end design effort versus fixed mask costs across process nodes.** Both curves contrast the shape of two cost classes across process nodes; neither reports measured program costs. Sourced design-cost anchors appear in @sec-design-loop-no-longer-scales. Front-end effort is the cost methodology can compress; the reticle mask set is a fixed charge that falls due at tapeout regardless of synthesis methodology.
#| out-width: "100%"
#| fig-alt: "Line chart on one shared log axis plotting front-end engineering design labor cost and reticle mask set charge across process nodes from 90nm to 2nm. Both constructed curves rise with node advance, and the mask charge climbs faster, closing the gap with front-end cost so the fixed charge becomes most of what a tapeout commitment risks."

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from _python.plots import COLORS, apply_style
import numpy as np

apply_style()

# Constructed illustrative parameters: both curves contrast the divergence in shape
# between a front-end cost methodology can compress and a fixed mask cost it cannot.
# Sourced design-cost anchors appear in @sec-design-loop-no-longer-scales.
nodes = ["90nm", "45nm", "28nm", "16nm", "7nm", "3nm", "2nm"]
x = np.arange(len(nodes))

mask_cost_m = np.array([1.5, 4.2, 12.5, 28.0, 65.0, 120.0, 180.0])
conv_design_cost_m = np.array([8.0, 16.0, 32.0, 55.0, 95.0, 150.0, 210.0])

fig, ax1 = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.4, 3.8))
fig.subplots_adjust(left=0.13, right=0.96, top=0.88, bottom=0.20)

ax1.set_yscale("log")
l1 = ax1.plot(
    x,
    conv_design_cost_m,
    color=COLORS["blue"],
    linewidth=2.0,
    marker="o",
    markersize=5,
    label="Front-end design effort (methodology can move this)",

)
l3 = ax1.plot(
    x,
    mask_cost_m,
    color=COLORS["red"],
    linewidth=2.2,
    marker="^",
    markersize=5.5,
    label="Reticle mask set charge (methodology cannot)",
    zorder=4,
)

ax1.set_xlabel("Semiconductor Process Technology Node", fontsize=6.8, labelpad=6)
ax1.set_ylabel("Cost per project ($M, log scale)", fontsize=6.8, color=COLORS["ink"])
ax1.set_xticks(x)
ax1.set_xticklabels(nodes, fontsize=6.2)
ax1.set_ylim(1.0, 400)
ax1.tick_params(axis="both", labelsize=6.0, length=2.5, width=0.6, pad=2)
ax1.grid(True, color=COLORS["grid"], linewidth=0.55, zorder=0)

ax1.annotate(
    "Mask charge closes the gap,\nmaking fixed tooling the\nprimary tapeout risk",
    xy=(6.0, 180.0),
    xytext=(1.9, 150.0),
    arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="->", color=COLORS["constraints_ink"], lw=0.9),
    fontsize=6.2,

for spine in ["top"]:
```

The engineering consequence of these intersecting cost curves is a capital governance obligation that automation cannot relieve. Cheaper candidate generation actually raises rather than lowers the evidentiary bar before authorizing a tapeout freeze. High-speed automated exploration increases the volume of plausible but subtly defective candidates competing for non-recurring capital, making derating signoff and independent physical verification the only defense against a mask write-off.

The same obligation is where the economics of the whole approach are settled, because the budget a program can spend is set by the volume that will amortize it. A specialized part recovers its NRE over far fewer units than a general-purpose die, and a subsystem such as the Lighthouse sits at the small end of that range (@sec-design-cost-pressure). An AI-native design system that proposes higher-performing candidates while adding to the verification and evaluation work each candidate demands has moved cost out of the stage methodology can compress and into the stages it cannot, and it fails the economic test whatever its benchmark numbers say. It passes only when it reaches a defensible, silicon-ready decision inside the engineering budget the product's volume can support. The evidence test from @sec-moonshot already asks whether the complete approach reduced the total cost of a comparable result; the commitment authority asks the same question in the product's own units, pricing the signoff and review effort the search generated against the mask charge that falls due regardless.

::: {.callout-lighthouse title="The Lighthouse commitment remains open"}
**Context.** Deciding whether to freeze an L2 cache capacity or a 32-by-32 NPU array layout for a mobile XR subsystem is a binding architectural commitment.

**Status.** The prospective cache study halted before dispatch, and the executed array study evaluated only isolated GEMM cycles. Neither record provides the physical signoff, power modeling, or system-level checks required to authorize silicon implementation. Consequently, the technical recommendation is to leave the freeze and tapeout commitment undecided pending qualified checks across all eight requirement domains (@sec-intent-vs-spec).
:::

A tapeout plan for the Lighthouse implementation requires integrating five distinct classes of qualified specialist evidence:

1. **Physical verification:** design rule check (DRC) and layout versus schematic (LVS) results against selected foundry decks, recording deck identities, approved waivers, and unresolved violations.
2. **Timing qualification:** setup and hold analysis across declared process, voltage, and temperature (PVT) corners, extraction modes, and variation models.
3. **Power-integrity and reliability qualification:** dynamic and static voltage-drop ($IR$ drop), electromigration, and reliability checks under declared activity and package assumptions.
4. **Logic and implementation correspondence:** formal equivalence checking stating compared representations, assumptions, and out-of-proof transformations.
5. **Manufacturing test qualification:** design-for-test (DFT) and automatic test pattern generation (ATPG) coverage metrics against manufacturing-test targets, identifying fault models and residual coverage gaps.

Passing technical checks does not create legal protection, and neither technical nor legal review grants commitment authority by itself. Missing required evidence blocks the recommendation to advance, leaving the named commitment authority to decide whether an eligible design proceeds or returns for further physical qualification.

## Sustaining Architectural Ownership {#sec-sustaining-responsibility}

Architectural ownership is an active capability to interrogate and reopen design decisions throughout the system life cycle. Sustaining control requires preserving access to candidates, boundary constraints, rejected alternatives, simulation traces, and signoff reports spanning compute, interconnect, memory, and packaging subsystems. In high-consequence engineering, naming reviewers who lack access to decisive artifacts or halting authority places them in exactly the crumple zone described above [@Elish2019MoralCrumpleZones]. Automation bias further increases the risk of uncritically accepting flawed synthesis advice or overlooking subtle physical layout bugs [@SkitkaEtAl1999AutomationBias].

Sustaining challenge capacity requires concrete operational exercises. Engineering teams reproduce selective checks, inspect failed candidates, diagnose seeded logic and timing faults in CPU and NPU blocks, and require independent human diagnosis before viewing tool recommendations. Opaque external dependencies (black-box IP blocks, foundry PDKs, commercial EDA engines) do not absolve engineering responsibility. Tapeout commitments must record IP versions, interface invariants, independent cross-checks, and difficult-to-diagnose failure modes, ensuring that a vendor certificate never substitutes for an independent technical check.

Transferring architectural responsibility requires handing off the underlying technical basis:

1. **Candidate release identity and boundary:** stated design question, system boundaries, and baseline assumptions.
2. **Decisive results spectrum:** passed, failed, inconclusive, and missing results across CPU, NPU, memory, and packaging layers.
3. **Uncertainty and containment:** bounded remaining uncertainties and validated fallback paths.
4. **Invalidation conditions:** explicit shifts in workloads, software stacks, EDA versions, manufacturing processes, or interfaces that mandate reconsideration.

Transferred technical foundations dictate continuous monitoring priorities. Operating teams track CPU queue tail latencies, UCIe retry rates, LPDDR5 ECC error counts, NPU thermal throttling, and reset signatures, surfacing telemetry signals tied directly to boundary conditions capable of overturning architecture choices.

<!-- AUTHOR-THESIS DRAFT 2026-08-31: contract owns "reopening decisions"; the invalidation conditions were listed but the text never said who may reopen, on what evidence threshold, or how the record is amended -->
Any party with access to the record may raise an invalidation condition, but only the architect of record may reopen the technical recommendation, and only the named commitment authority may reopen the commitment that rested on it. The threshold is a telemetry signal or fresh check that falls outside a condition the record declared as covered, one of the invalidation conditions above met in fact, or a qualified check that contradicts a result the recommendation relied on; a worse-looking dashboard is not enough. Reopening appends to the record rather than editing it, so the original recommendation, decision, and evidence stand as written, a dated entry names the trigger and who invoked it, and any revised recommendation and decision follow as new entries in the same serial order that governed the first.
<!-- END DRAFT -->

## Architectural Alignment Under Team Churn {#sec-sustaining-alignment-churn}

Maintaining architectural integrity across continuous engineering churn is a central responsibility of the lead architect in industrial organizations. When distributed teams push daily commits to RTL repositories, device drivers, compiler backends, and firmware stacks, an architectural recommendation formulated against last month's repository snapshot can quietly become invalid. Sustaining ownership under high-velocity churn requires active governance rather than periodic, ceremonial signoff.

To prevent moving-target invalidation, the architect establishes continuous differential validation within production integration pipelines. The design system must revalidate generated proposals against daily integration branches through continuous equivalence and timing checks, catching interface regressions before recommendations reach commitment review. When delegating subblock optimization to automated optimizers, the architect specifies strict locality-of-modification contracts. These boundary invariants restrict the tool from altering external bus protocols, clock-domain crossings, or register-map addresses, ensuring that changes remain locally verifiable and cleanly mergeable with daily developer commits.

Run-to-run dispersion serves as an early indicator of microarchitectural fragility. If an automated tuning pass produces high-performing RTL on one seed but fails timing closure or routability on another, the candidate represents a physically brittle design rather than a robust microarchitecture. Tracking dispersion across continuous integration runs ensures that only candidate designs with demonstrated stability across the parameter distribution receive authorization to advance toward tapeout. When unexpected failures escape into silicon, they force commitments open again. The Pentium FDIV bug [@Edelman1997PentiumDivision] showed how an escaped flaw invalidates release confidence and demands renewed architecture work, containment, and a recall or replacement decision.

## Closing the Moonshot {#sec-closing-moonshot}

We opened this book with an ambition stated in one breath: design a low-power, 64-bit RISC-V-based compute subsystem for a real-time mobile XR workload. That prompt anchored our running Lighthouse study across eleven chapters. We used it to test intent representation, prompt decomposition, domain-specific state spaces, multi-tool orchestration, verification feedback, cross-stack transfer, and system-level evaluation.

We can now state what the book's own records establish. The prospective cache study (@sec-running-the-loop) halted before dispatch when its declared constraints and trace budgets were unmet. The executed array study (@sec-running-the-loop) evaluated isolated GEMM cycle counts on synthetic kernels, but omitted physical timing closure, PDN $IR$-drop modeling, 3\ W thermal envelopes, compiler lowering paths, and full-system software fallbacks.

Against our two closing tests, the verdict is plain:

1. **Program claim status.** Against our first test, the Lighthouse program claim is *unresolved*. It does not mean the approach failed, and it is not a polite way of saying the approach succeeded. It means the decisive empirical measurements required to justify a commitment (transient PDN voltage droop under bursty vector execution, full-stack MLIR/Triton compiler lowering, UCIe die-to-die PHY thermal dissipation, and formal equivalence across out-of-proof transformations) were never taken, and the post-silicon containment path through hardware chicken-bits was never verified. Naming the missing measurement is what makes this an architecture result rather than a shrug.
2. **Architecture commitment.** Against our second test, no tapeout commitment packet was ever authorized or submitted. Forcing a commitment verdict from the held evidence would have demonstrated the exact failure this chapter exists to prevent: an architecture commitment made by implication because an automated workflow ran to completion and produced something that looked like an answer.

What the book establishes does not depend on how the Lighthouse turned out. The framework is the deliverable; the Lighthouse was the test case that kept it honest. There is a temptation, in a book that argues for AI-native system design, to close on a triumphant demonstration that the method works. A clean win on our own running example, scored by us, against a baseline we chose, would have been the weakest evidence in the book. Architecture 2.0 is not a claim that autonomy is solved; it is the discipline of building AI-native design systems and holding them to an architecture-grade evidence standard.

::: {.callout-design-principle title="Delegate Execution, Retain Accountability"}
**The principle:** While automated design systems execute exploration, optimization, and synthesis across the stack, human architects retain nondelegable accountability for problem framing, abstraction selection, residual risk declaration, and the supported technical recommendation. A named commitment authority remains accountable for deciding whether the organization makes an irreversible capital commitment.

**The application:** Every architectural transition must trace back to a named commitment authority within an accountable organization, backed by explicit reopening triggers and verified containment paths.
:::

## Common Pitfalls {#sec-ownership-pitfalls}

These are an organization's errors rather than an engineer's. Each one loses a decision's owner somewhere between tool execution and reticle mask commitment:

- **Committing to an unpriced workflow:** Adopting or rejecting an automated workflow without accounting for tool compute costs, closure effort, review load, and resulting artifact quality.
- **Treating clean tool exits as signoff authority:** Treating zero-exit status from a bounded optimizer as authorization to proceed, confusing local constraint satisfaction with cross-layer signoff.
- **Unverified black-box IP signoff:** Accepting third-party or generated IP on top-level pass rates without verifying interface invariants with independent boundary checkers.
- **Normalization of deviance in synthesis workarounds:** Approving repeated constraint waivers without expiration dates, containment plans, or post-silicon validation checks.
- **Piecemeal domain signoff:** Approving system assembly by aggregating isolated domain approvals without checking cross-domain thermal, power delivery, and interconnect coupling at the seams.
- **Detaching diagnostics at tapeout:** Archiving simulation infrastructure and cross-layer models upon mask release, eliminating the diagnostic apparatus needed to trace post-silicon anomalies.

## Open Questions

Five questions remain open once ownership is structured this way:

- **How do you isolate a fault across chiplet boundaries without exposing proprietary IP?** Multi-die 2.5D and 3D assemblies integrate chiplets from distinct commercial vendors across high-speed interconnects like UCIe. When intermittent data corruption occurs, determining whether the root cause lies in the CPU memory interface, interposer channel impedance, or NPU DMA controller requires fine-grained internal telemetry that vendors refuse to publish. Whether standardized, zero-knowledge telemetry interfaces can isolate seam faults mathematically, or multi-vendor chiplet packaging forces legal joint-liability pacts that cannot be verified through technical telemetry alone, defines the multi-die governance boundary.

- **Where must on-chip diagnostic monitors sit when you cannot afford to instrument every wire?** Post-silicon anomalies, including transient voltage droop, clock jitter, and race conditions, require hardware diagnostic monitors to trace root causes on test benches. Instrumenting every clock domain and bus interface consumes prohibitive silicon area and routing tracks. Whether analytical sensor placement algorithms can mathematically guarantee fault disambiguation with minimal physical taps, or architects must accept unmonitored blind spots and rely on firmware chicken-bits when anomalies arise, defines the post-silicon observability trade-off.

- **When does a stack of harmless constraint waivers become a tapeout failure?** In the final sprint before mask release, teams approve dozens of local timing, DRC, and false-path waivers to meet schedule commitments. While each waiver appears benign in isolation, their joint interaction across supply-voltage fluctuations and process variations creates systemic failure modes that static tools miss. Whether probabilistic waiver-density models can establish formal thresholds that trigger automated tapeout halts, or waiver signoff remains an irreducibly subjective judgment call that human commitment authorities must personally own, defines the residual risk boundary.

- **How do junior architects learn to make decisions when machines do all the design work?** AI-native design systems automate RTL drafting, constraint tuning, and timing closure. When junior engineers interact with chip design only through natural language prompts and high-level scorecards, they never build the tacit physical intuition required to diagnose subtle signoff anomalies or serve as future commitment authorities. Whether structured pedagogical verification regimens and synthetic fault-injection environments can train diagnostic judgment synthetically, or automation will create a generational competence gap where no human understands the physical substrate well enough to own a capital commitment, is the central organizational dilemma.

- **What constitutes legally defensible evidence when an automatically generated design fails in the field?** Automated generators produce complex, non-human-authored microarchitectures that pass all pre-silicon signoff checks. When an unmodeled security vulnerability or intermittent physical fault causes a fatal automotive or medical system failure, standard product liability requires proving due care and defect traceability. Whether versioned study records and cryptographic proof chains satisfy legal standards of engineering diligence, or courts will treat machine-generated hardware under strict liability doctrines that no verification artifact can mitigate, defines the legal frontier of automated design.

## Summary

Architectural ownership in an era of automated design rests on explicit governance boundaries, provenance tracking, and nondelegable human stewardship. While machine learning models accelerate artifact drafting, parameter optimization, and formal property generation, they do not carry organizational accountability. When a chip fails in silicon or produces a field recall, responsibility cannot be attributed to an algorithm, a container hash, or a foundation model prompt.

Trustworthy ownership requires an in-order handoff from execution and scoped support to the architect's system recommendation and the named authority's recorded commitment decision, together with continuous differential validation against moving mainline codebases and verified post-silicon containment.

::: {.callout-takeaways}
- **Nondelegable commitment authority.** Automated tools and domain specialists propose and qualify local designs, architects form the supported system recommendation, and named human commitment authorities retain exclusive, nondelegable authority over irreversible capital allocation and tapeout freezes.
- **In-order commit discipline and three-tier authority.** Exploration may speculate across parallel design branches, but specification changes, constraint waivers, and baseline promotions must be resolved in strict serial order, decoupling execution, analytical support, and strategic commitment.
- **Pre-silicon derating and chicken-bit containment.** Proposed chicken-bits require a verified safe state, empirical characterization of the implemented control's performance penalty, compatible control combinations, and checks that the candidate preserves the declared requirements under the tested derated envelope ($\Delta_{\text{derate}}$).
- **Continuous differential validation.** Mitigate moving-target engineering churn through continuous differential validation and locality-of-modification contracts, so that a recommendation formulated against one repository snapshot is revalidated before it reaches commitment review.
:::

Several limits this chapter reached, unpriced compute, missing benchmark governance, and closed signoff decks among them, are shared across the discipline rather than local to one team, and @sec-bootstrapping-ecosystem asks what the discipline would have to build for any team to record a better verdict.
